---
title: "Quiz: linear classifiers"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A linear classifier decides by the sign of $f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b$; labels are $y = \pm 1$.

---

**Q1.** Give one example each of a classification problem where the points are pixels, objects and image windows. What are the features?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is measured for each pixel, each object, each window?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pixels: nucleus / cytoplasm / background, with features from a stack of filtered images (smoothed intensity at several scales, edge strength, blob and texture responses). Objects: cell / debris, with features from the measurement table (area, mean intensity, form factor). Windows: "cell here" / "no cell", with a descriptor of the patch (e.g. histograms of gradient directions). In all three each item becomes a point in a feature space with a label.
:::

---

**Q2.** For $f(\mathbf x) = 2x_1 - x_2 + 1$, which side is class $+1$? What is the signed distance of $(0, 3)$ to the line?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The distance is $f/\|\mathbf w\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Class $+1$ is the side $\mathbf w = (2, -1)$ points to (right and down). $f(0, 3) = 0 - 3 + 1 = -2$, $\|\mathbf w\| = \sqrt5$, distance $-2/\sqrt5 = -0.894$: the point lies on the $-1$ side, 0.894 from the line.
:::

---

**Q3.** You multiply $\mathbf w$ and $b$ by 10. Which of these change: the line, the classification of each point, the value of $f$, the distance of each point to the line?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write $f/\|\mathbf w\|$ for the scaled classifier.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only the value of $f$ (ten times larger). The line $f = 0$, the signs (classes) and the distances $f/\|\mathbf w\|$ are unchanged. So the value of $f$ alone means nothing until the scale of $(\mathbf w, b)$ is fixed.
:::

---

**Q4.** The two class means are $\boldsymbol\mu_+ = (2, 2)$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_- = (0, 0)$. Give the nearest-class-mean line.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Perpendicular to $\boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-$, through the midpoint.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathbf w = (2, 2)$, midpoint $(1, 1)$, $b = -(2 + 2) = -4$: $f = 2x_1 + 2x_2 - 4$, the line $x_1 + x_2 = 2$.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two long, thin, parallel clouds are shifted mostly along their length. Why does the nearest-class-mean line do badly, even though a line with zero errors exists?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
In which direction does $\boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-$ point?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-$ points mostly along the clouds, so the nearest-mean line, perpendicular to it, runs across both clouds and cuts them. The separating line runs **along** the clouds, through the narrow gap. Nearest mean only looks at the two means, not at the shape of the clouds.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why can no line separate a nucleus (inside) from the cytoplasm around it when the features are the pixel's $(x, y)$ position, or two intensity features in which the cytoplasm surrounds the nucleus?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A line splits the plane into two half-planes. Can a half-plane contain the inside of a ring but not the ring?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A half-plane is convex and unbounded: if it contains the inner blob it also contains every point on the far side, including part of the ring, because the ring surrounds the blob in all directions. A ring around a blob needs a closed boundary (a circle), which a linear classifier on these two features cannot produce. Adding a feature such as the squared distance from the centre makes it linear again (unit 3).
:::

---

**Q7.** Is the SVM generative or discriminative? And a classifier that fits one Gaussian per class and picks the more likely class?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does the method describe how each class is distributed?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The SVM is **discriminative**: it only looks for a boundary. The Gaussian-per-class classifier is **generative**: it models each class and compares likelihoods (the minimum-error threshold of the thresholding day is the 1D case; the Gaussian mixtures day goes further).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that $f(\mathbf x)/\|\mathbf w\|$ is the same for $(\mathbf w, b)$ and $(c\mathbf w, cb)$ with $c > 0$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\|c\mathbf w\| = |c|\,\|\mathbf w\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(c\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + cb)/\|c\mathbf w\| = c(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b)/(c\|\mathbf w\|) = f(\mathbf x)/\|\mathbf w\|$ for $c > 0$. For $c < 0$ the sign flips: the same line, the sides swapped.
:::
